To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Alfuy subtype of MVEV is highly attenuated for neuroinvasion in mice and that the prM and E proteins are responsible for this attenuation, and that the hinge region and glycosylation site in E are two motifs that contribute to attenuation.

the Alfuy strain of Murray Valley encephlaitis virus is attenuated in weanling mouse models and that this attenuation is due, at least in part, to the presence of unique amino acid sequences within the Alfuy E protein.
we have identified the structural genes of ALFV as the attenuating factors and the hinge region of E protein as a major attenuating factor of the virus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and analysis of the molecular determinants of virulence in a mosquito-borne alphavirus, Murray Valley encephalis virus (MVE).
the identification of viral factors that contribute to the neuroinvasiveness of the encephalitic MVEV and the attenuation of ALFU virus.
the molecular mechanisms of viral attenuation and the identification of attenuated strains that can be used as vaccine vectors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ALFV is attenuated by virtue of the unique hinge sequence and lack of a glycosylation site on its E protein.
the ALFV E protein is attenuated by virtue of its sequence and that the hinge region is a major attenuating factor in ALFV.
the ALFV prM and E genes, when swapped into a highly neuroinvasive virus, such as MVEV, result in a significantly less neurovirulent virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the E protein is a major determinant of neuroinvasiveness in MVEV, and that the ALFV E protein has mutations that reduce its neuroinvasive potential in weanling BALB/c mice.

we have identified the structural genes prM/E as the region that is responsible for the attenuation of ALV, and that the E protein glycosylated at position 154 and the hinge region (res. 273-277, 279-281) are important determinants of attenuation in this virus.
the ALFV E protein has unique amino acid substitutions at residues 154 and 273-277, which are associated with reduced neuroinvasiveness and attenuation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hinge and the glycosylation site are both important in determining the virulence of the flavivirus.
we have identified two viral motifs in the E protein that are associated with attenuation in mice, and we propose that these motifs are also associated with the attenuation of ALFU virus in humans.

the E protein of Alfuy is a major determinant of attenuation in the mouse model of encephalitic disease, and that there are at least two distinct regions within the E protein that are important for this phenotype.
